body:
Why semiconductor doping matters

Silicon is a widely used semiconductor. Its conductivity can be changed substantially by adding very small amounts of selected elements. This intentional process is called doping.

The 2 important categories of doped semiconductor are n-type and p-type. The distinction depends on which mobile charge carriers are more abundant.

N-type: electrons are the majority carriers

In an n-type semiconductor, added impurity atoms provide extra electrons that can take part in conduction. For silicon, a suitable example is phosphorus, which has 5 valence electrons, compared with silicon's 4.

In this arrangement, electrons are the majority carriers. The letter n refers to negative charge carriers. It does not mean that the whole semiconductor has a net negative electrical charge.

P-type: holes are the majority carriers

In a p-type semiconductor, suitable impurity atoms lead to an increased number of holes. Boron, which has 3 valence electrons, is a common example of a dopant for silicon.

Holes behave as positive charge carriers and are the majority carriers in p-type material. The letter p refers to these positive carriers, not to a permanent positive charge on the entire material.

PropertyN-typeP-type
Example dopant in siliconPhosphorusBoron
Majority carrierElectronsHoles
Minority carrierHolesElectrons
Overall bulk chargeElectrically neutralElectrically neutral

Both n-type and p-type semiconductor materials are electrically neutral overall. Their names describe the dominant mobile charge carriers.

A p-n junction makes controlled current flow possible

When a p-type region and an n-type region meet inside a semiconductor device, they form a p-n junction. Charge carriers redistribute near the boundary, producing a depletion region with few mobile charge carriers and a potential barrier that restricts current flow unless the applied electrical conditions are suitable.

A basic semiconductor diode is a 2-terminal device built around a junction of this kind. It allows current to pass much more readily in one direction than in the opposite direction.

Forward bias

For an ordinary p-n junction diode, forward bias means that the p-side is connected towards the positive side of the applied voltage and the n-side towards the negative side. Under a suitable forward voltage, the diode conducts appreciable current.

Reverse bias

In reverse bias, the p-side is connected towards the negative side of the applied voltage and the n-side towards the positive side. Under normal operating conditions, the diode largely blocks current, although a small leakage current may remain.

This directional behaviour makes a rectifier diode useful in converting alternating current (AC), whose direction periodically reverses, into direct current (DC), which flows in one direction in the external circuit.

LEDs convert electrical energy into light

An LED is a light-emitting diode. When a suitable LED is forward biased, electrons and holes recombine in its semiconductor material and energy is emitted as light.

An LED is therefore a special type of diode that serves as a light source. Ordinary rectifier diodes are primarily used to control current direction, not to provide visible illumination.

LEDs are used in indicator lights, displays, traffic signals and energy-efficient lighting. Many LEDs can produce useful light with much less heating of the surroundings than an incandescent filament bulb of comparable light output.

In a common through-hole indicator LED, the longer lead is generally the positive lead, or anode, while the shorter lead is generally the negative lead, or cathode. Lead length is a recognition aid for many such components, not a universal rule for every LED package.

A semiconductor LED is different from an ordinary filament bulb. A filament bulb glows because its wire becomes very hot; an LED produces light through an electronic process in the semiconductor.

Prelims focus

  • N-type semiconductor: electrons are majority carriers.
  • P-type semiconductor: holes are majority carriers.
  • Phosphorus is a familiar n-type dopant for silicon; boron is a familiar p-type dopant.
  • A diode is a 2-terminal device that conducts readily in one direction.
  • LED stands for light-emitting diode and produces light during suitable forward conduction.
  • Rectifier diodes are used in AC-to-DC conversion.
  • Trap: The term p-type does not mean that the whole material is positively charged.

[OpenStax, University Physics Volume 3, sections 9.6, Semiconductors and Doping, and 9.7, Semiconductor Devices, consulted 3 November 2026; NCERT, Physics Laboratory Manual, Class 12, Activity 8, identification of diodes, LEDs and transistors; NCERT, Science, Class 8, 2018-19 edition, Chapter 14, Chemical Effects of Electric Current, printed pp. 174-175.]

body:
A transistor controls electrical current

A transistor is a semiconductor device that can control a larger electrical current or signal through a smaller controlling signal. This ability makes it useful in electronic switching and amplification.

A basic bipolar junction transistor has 3 terminals called the emitter, base and collector. The base is associated with the controlling signal, while the transistor controls current through the other part of its circuit. Different transistor technologies use different terminal names, but the common elementary idea is controlled switching or amplification.

As a switch, a transistor can turn current through a component on or off electronically. As an amplifier, it can produce a larger output signal from a smaller input signal using energy supplied by the circuit.

Modern processors and memory chips contain enormous numbers of transistors. Their switching action is one of the foundations of digital electronics.

How a transistor differs from a diode

An ordinary diode is mainly a 2-terminal device used to permit current much more readily in one direction. A transistor generally has 3 terminals and is used to control current or amplify a signal.

Both are semiconductor devices, but their primary functions are not interchangeable. A diode used for rectification is not simply a small transistor, and a transistor is not merely a diode with an extra wire.

A solar cell converts light into electricity

A solar photovoltaic cell, also called a solar cell, uses a semiconductor to convert light energy directly into electrical energy. Silicon is the most widely used semiconductor material in conventional solar cells.

When suitable light is absorbed in the semiconductor, it can make additional charge carriers available. The device's internal electrical properties help separate charges so that an electric current can flow through an external circuit.

Solar photovoltaic cells generate direct current (DC). A grid-connected solar power system commonly uses an inverter to convert this into alternating current (AC).

A solar cell is not a miniature nuclear reactor. It uses energy arriving as sunlight. Although sunlight is called solar radiation, the normal photovoltaic effect does not require radioactive material or nuclear fission inside the panel.

LED and solar cell: opposite energy-conversion directions

An LED uses electrical energy and emits light. A solar cell absorbs light energy and produces electrical energy. Both use semiconductor properties, but they are designed for different purposes.

DevicePrimary functionFamiliar application
DiodePermits current mainly in 1 directionRectifier
LEDConverts electrical energy into lightLighting and indicators
TransistorControls or amplifies current and signalsDigital circuits and amplifiers
Solar cellConverts light into electrical energySolar panels

Semiconductors in India's technology programmes

The India Semiconductor Mission (ISM), associated with the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, supports the development of India's semiconductor ecosystem. The Semicon India Programme includes initiatives related to semiconductor manufacturing, assembly, testing, packaging and design.

Semiconductor manufacturing and semiconductor packaging are related but different activities. A fabrication facility, commonly called a fab, manufactures semiconductor devices on wafers. Assembly, testing and packaging operations prepare and verify semiconductor products for their intended use. The existence of a packaging facility does not automatically mean that wafer fabrication is taking place at the same location.

In official information issued on 17 September 2026, Semicon 2.0 was described as a phase intended to strengthen areas including semiconductor design, equipment, materials, fabrication, packaging, research and workforce development. These are programme priorities rather than separate physical properties of semiconductor materials.

Gujarat: Dholera and Sanand

Dholera, Gujarat, is an important location in India's semiconductor manufacturing plans. The Government of India announced on 16 April 2026 that a special economic zone associated with Tata Semiconductor Manufacturing Private Limited had been notified at Dholera. The official announcement concerned the establishment of a semiconductor fabrication project.

A Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology release dated 17 September 2026 reported that construction of the Dholera semiconductor fabrication facility was on track. Therefore, at the 3 November 2026 content cutoff, the cited official status is under construction; it should not be described as an already operating commercial wafer fabrication plant on the basis of those releases.

The same September 2026 official communication reported that commercial DRAM and NAND production was live at Sanand, Gujarat. This is a separate development from the Dholera fabrication project. The names of these locations are useful for connecting semiconductor concepts with Gujarat's industrial development, but their project stages must not be confused.

Putting the whole subtopic together

The concepts in this lesson belong to connected but distinct areas of science. Atomic structure explains protons, neutrons, electrons and isotopes. Nuclear processes explain radioactivity, fission and fusion. Electrical properties of materials explain why copper conducts, rubber insulates and silicon can be used to control current. Semiconductor devices apply that controlled conduction in diodes, LEDs, transistors and solar cells.

The applications also differ. Fission releases nuclear energy for electricity generation; radioactive isotopes support selected medical treatments and examinations; semiconductor devices control electricity, produce light or convert sunlight into electricity.

Prelims focus

  • A basic bipolar transistor has emitter, base and collector terminals.
  • Diodes, LEDs, transistors and solar cells use semiconductor properties for different functions.
  • An LED converts electricity into light; a photovoltaic cell converts sunlight into electricity.
  • India Semiconductor Mission is associated with the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology.
  • The Dholera fab was reported under construction on 17 September 2026.
  • Commercial memory-product production at Sanand was reported in the same September 2026 official communication.
  • Trap: A solar cell does not generate electricity through nuclear fission, and a semiconductor packaging facility is not automatically a wafer fabrication plant.

[NCERT, Physics Laboratory Manual, Class 12, Activity 8, identification of semiconductor components and transistor terminals; OpenStax, University Physics Volume 3, section 9.7, Semiconductor Devices, consulted 3 November 2026; US Department of Energy, Solar Photovoltaic Cell Basics, section What Is a Solar Photovoltaic Cell?, consulted 3 November 2026; Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Commerce and Industry, Government Notifies India's First Chip Fabrication Plant at SEZ Dholera, 16 April 2026; Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, SEMICON India 2026 release on semiconductor production and Semicon 2.0, 17 September 2026. Official project statuses stated for the 3 November 2026 cutoff.]
